lead: Memphis plumbing deals with clay soil, old neighborhoods, summer storms and the occasional hard freeze. PipeMend sends licensed local plumbers across Memphis.
risk: cracked sewer lines in shifting clay, aging pipes in older homes and frozen pipes
risk_short: sewer lines, old pipes and frozen pipes
why: Midtown and Cooper-Young have homes from the early 1900s, with galvanized supply lines and clay or cast-iron sewer laterals. The area's clay soil moves with wet and dry seasons and cracks those lines.
Hard freezes, like the one in December 2022, burst pipes in crawl spaces and exterior walls. Heavy storms back up drains in low areas.
water: MLGW pumps water from the Memphis Sand Aquifer, known for its quality. The water is soft and needs little treatment.
tips: Scope the sewer line before buying an older home.
Know where your main shutoff is.
Drip faucets in a hard freeze.
areas: PipeMend works in Midtown, Cooper-Young, East Memphis, Downtown, Whitehaven, Hickory Hill and every other Memphis neighborhood.
permits: Plumbing permits for Memphis come from Shelby County Code Enforcement, which also handles local plumber licensing. Larger jobs may also need a Tennessee contractor license.

faq.a: No. Memphis water comes from the Memphis Sand Aquifer and is soft. Scale is less of a problem than in most cities, though water heaters still benefit from a yearly flush.
